80.uses: Japanese crab apple is one of the most profusely flowering small trees. It is used in residential streets, parks, school yards, residential developments and gardens. The small yellow-red fruits stay on the branches in autumn and feed birds.
80.planting: It reaches 4–6 m with a broad, rounded crown. In avenues it is planted 5–6 m apart. It prefers full sun and fertile, well-drained soils. Plant in autumn or spring.
80.care: Water regularly in the first years. Pruning is limited to dead or crossing branches, after flowering. It is very frost-hardy (to about -30°C).

faq.q: When does Japanese crab apple flower?
faq.a: In April, with pink buds and masses of white-pink flowers.

faq.q: Do ornamental crab apples produce fruit?
faq.a: Yes, small decorative fruits that stay on the branches in autumn and feed birds.

81.uses: Staghorn sumac is valued for its autumn colour, among the most intense of all shrubs, and for the exotic look of its pinnate leaves. It is used on slopes, in modern gardens, in public spaces with poor soils and as a specimen. The red velvety fruit clusters stay on the branches over winter.
81.planting: It reaches 3–5 m in height and width. It prefers full sun and adapts to almost any soil, including sandy or poor ones. It produces root suckers and spreads, so a root barrier is recommended next to paths and beds.
81.care: It tolerates drought and heat very well and needs no special care. Unwanted suckers are removed periodically. It is very frost-hardy.

faq.q: Does staghorn sumac spread?
faq.a: Yes, it produces root suckers; a root barrier is recommended next to paths and beds.

faq.q: When is staghorn sumac most decorative?
faq.a: In autumn, when the leaves turn intense red-orange.

82.uses: Bluebeard flowers at the end of summer, when few shrubs are still in flower, bringing a rare blue to planting schemes. It is used in borders, sunny beds, gravel gardens, pollinator gardens and in combination with ornamental grasses and lavender.
82.planting: It reaches 60–100 cm. Plant 3–4 plants per square metre. It needs full sun and well-drained, even dry soil; it does not tolerate waterlogging.
82.care: In spring, as growth starts, cut plants back to 15–20 cm above the ground – it flowers on new wood. In very cold winters the shoots may freeze back, but the plant regrows from the base. It tolerates drought well.

faq.q: When does bluebeard flower?
faq.a: At the end of summer, usually in August–September.

faq.q: How is bluebeard pruned?
faq.a: In spring, to 15–20 cm above the ground, as the flowers appear on new shoots.

83.uses: Kerria is one of the few flowering shrubs that does well in partial and full shade. It is used in borders, under trees, on the north side of buildings, in residential gardens and parks. Its green, arching stems stay decorative in winter.
83.planting: It reaches 1.5–2 m. Plant 1–2 plants per square metre or 2 per linear metre for informal borders. It adapts to most soils and tolerates sun, partial and full shade.
83.care: After flowering remove the oldest stems at the base to rejuvenate. It spreads by suckers, so limit it when needed. It is hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Does kerria grow in shade?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the few flowering shrubs that tolerates partial and full shade well.

faq.q: When does Japanese kerria flower?
faq.a: In April–May, with golden-yellow, often double flowers.

84.uses: Forsythia is the herald of spring: it flowers among the first shrubs, when gardens are still bare. It is used in informal hedges, park groups, on slopes, in public spaces and residential gardens, often combined with later-flowering shrubs.
84.planting: It reaches 2–3 m. For informal hedges plant 1–2 plants per linear metre, in groups 1–1.5 m apart. It adapts to almost any soil and prefers sun, where it flowers most freely.
84.care: Prune right after flowering, removing some of the old stems at the base; pruning in autumn or winter removes the flower buds. It is very robust and easy to maintain.

faq.q: When should forsythia be pruned?
faq.a: Right after flowering; autumn or winter pruning removes the flower buds.

faq.q: Can forsythia be used as a hedge?
faq.a: Yes, especially as an informal flowering hedge, with 1–2 plants per metre.

85.uses: Snowberry is a safe choice for public green spaces: borders, low hedges, slopes, shaded areas under trees and parks. The decorative white berries stay on the branches for much of the winter. The berries are not edible and may cause discomfort if eaten.
85.planting: It reaches 1–2 m. For low hedges plant 2–3 plants per linear metre, for areas 1–2 per square metre. It adapts to almost any soil, including poor ones, and tolerates sun and shade.
85.care: It is extremely frost-hardy and tolerant of urban conditions. Trim in spring and remove old stems periodically. It spreads by suckers, which makes it good for stabilising slopes.

faq.q: Are snowberry berries edible?
faq.a: No; the white berries are decorative but not edible and may cause discomfort.

faq.q: Does snowberry grow in shade?
faq.a: Yes, it tolerates shade well, including under trees.

86.uses: Cotton lavender is grown for its silver foliage, decorative all year, which contrasts with green or purple plants. It is planted in low clipped or informal edging, rock and gravel gardens, sunny slopes and with lavender and ornamental grasses.
86.planting: It reaches 30–50 cm. Plant 5–7 plants per square metre or 3–4 per linear metre for edging. It needs full sun and poor, dry, very well-drained soil.
86.care: After flowering trim the plants to keep them compact; trim lightly in spring. It tolerates drought very well but dislikes excess winter wet. Hardy to about -15°C.

faq.q: Where should cotton lavender be planted?
faq.a: In sunny sites on dry, well-drained soil, in edging, gravel gardens and Mediterranean gardens.

faq.q: Can cotton lavender be clipped as edging?
faq.a: Yes, it tolerates trimming well and forms low silver edging.

87.uses: European larch is a conifer that loses its needles in winter – completely normal for this species. It is used in parks, groups, large green spaces, shelterbelts and mountain areas, where its golden autumn colour is striking.
87.planting: It reaches 25–35 m with an airy conical crown. Plant as a specimen or in groups 4–6 m apart. It prefers full sun and moist, well-drained soils; it does not tolerate waterlogging.
87.care: It is very frost-hardy. Water regularly in the first years, especially in dry summers. No pruning is needed. In winter, without needles, the tree is not dead – it leafs out again in spring.

faq.q: Is it normal for larch to lose its needles in winter?
faq.a: Yes, larch is a deciduous conifer; the needles drop in autumn and regrow in spring.

faq.q: Where should larch be planted?
faq.a: In sunny sites with moist, well-drained soil, in parks and large green spaces.

88.uses: Holly is valued for its glossy foliage, green all year, and its red berries, decorative in the cold season. It is used in dense, hard-to-pass hedges, shaded areas, at entrances, as a specimen or clipped into shapes. Berries appear only on female plants with a male plant nearby, and they are not edible.
88.planting: For hedges plant 2–3 plants per linear metre. It tolerates sun and shade and prefers acidic to neutral, moist, well-drained soils. Shelter it from cold, drying winter winds.
88.care: It grows slowly and is trimmed in summer. Water regularly during dry spells in the first years. It is hardy to about -20°C. Wear gloves when working with it because of the spiny leaves.

faq.q: Why is my holly not producing berries?
faq.a: Berries appear only on female plants, and only if there is a male plant nearby for pollination.

faq.q: Does holly grow in shade?
faq.a: Yes, holly tolerates shade and partial shade well.

89.uses: Himalayan pine stands out with needles up to 15–20 cm long, in bundles of five, giving the crown a soft, almost fluffy look. It is used as a specimen in parks, large gardens, company headquarters and residential developments, contrasting nicely with short-needled conifers.
89.planting: In cultivation it usually reaches 15–20 m with a broad conical crown. Plant as a specimen with plenty of room. It prefers sunny sites sheltered from cold, drying winds and well-drained soils.
89.care: Water regularly in the first years, especially in summer. No pruning is needed. It is hardy to about -25°C; cold winter winds can brown the needle tips on exposed trees.

faq.q: What makes Himalayan pine distinctive?
faq.a: Its very long, soft, blue-green, slightly drooping needles and long cones.

faq.q: Where should Himalayan pine be planted?
faq.a: As a specimen in sun, sheltered from cold winds, on well-drained soil.

90.uses: Mountain pine grows naturally in the alpine zone and is one of the toughest conifers for landscaping. It is used in rock gardens, on slopes, roundabouts, intensive green roofs, planters and roadsides, where it tolerates wind and even salt.
90.planting: Depending on variety it reaches 1–3 m in height and width. Plant 1–1.5 m apart for compact groups. It prefers full sun and well-drained soils, including poor or calcareous ones.
90.care: In spring the new shoots ('candles') can be shortened by a third to a half for a more compact shape. Once established it tolerates drought and frost very well. No other care is needed.

faq.q: How big does mountain pine grow?
faq.a: Depending on variety, usually 1–3 m in height and width.

faq.q: How do you keep mountain pine compact?
faq.a: By shortening the new shoots in spring by a third to a half.

91.uses: The 'Brepo' variety (also sold as 'Pierrick Bregeon') keeps the toughness of black pine in a compact, rounded form. It is used in terrace pots, rock and gravel gardens, green roofs, dwarf conifer borders and at entrances as a geometric accent.
91.planting: It grows very slowly, usually reaching about 60–100 cm in ten years. Plant 70–100 cm apart in groups. It prefers full sun and well-drained soils; in pots use a free-draining compost.
91.care: It is very tolerant of frost, wind and drought and needs no pruning – the globe shape is natural. In pots water regularly in summer without waterlogging.

faq.q: How big does black pine 'Brepo' grow?
faq.a: It grows very slowly, usually about 60–100 cm in ten years, keeping its round shape.

faq.q: Can 'Brepo' be grown in a pot?
faq.a: Yes, it is very well suited to pots and planters with a well-drained compost.

92.uses: Lombardy poplar is one of the fastest solutions for tall screens against wind, dust and view around farms, warehouses, industrial zones and large plots. It is also used in rows along roads and canals as a vertical landscape accent.
92.planting: It reaches 25–30 m but stays narrow. For screens plant 2–4 m apart, in rows 4–6 m. It adapts to most soils and tolerates moist ones. Its roots are strong and extensive, so plant it well away from buildings, pipes and foundations.
92.care: It grows very fast in the first years and needs little care. It is very frost-hardy. It has a shorter lifespan than other park trees; dead branches are removed periodically.

faq.q: How fast does Lombardy poplar grow?
faq.a: Very fast – it is one of the fastest trees for windbreaks.

faq.q: How far from buildings should poplar be planted?
faq.a: Well away from buildings, pipes and foundations, as its roots are strong and extensive.

93.uses: Hardy geranium is one of the most reliable perennials for ground cover in public and private green spaces: under trees, in borders, on slopes, in shady gardens and with roses and shrubs. Some species, such as Geranium macrorrhizum, have aromatic leaves and stay almost green in winter.
93.planting: Plant 6–8 plants per square metre. It tolerates sun, partial and full shade and adapts to most soils, including dry ones. It quickly forms a dense carpet that suppresses weeds.
93.care: After the first flush of flowers the plants can be cut back for repeat flowering and compact foliage. It needs no feeding or regular watering once established. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Is hardy geranium the same as the balcony geranium?
faq.a: No; hardy geranium is a frost-hardy garden perennial, while the balcony geranium (Pelargonium) does not survive winter outdoors.

faq.q: Does hardy geranium grow in shade?
faq.a: Yes, many species tolerate partial and full shade well, including under trees.

94.uses: Japanese blood grass brings a rare colour to planting: its upright leaves gradually turn red from spring to autumn and seem to glow when backlit. It is used in borders, mass planting, modern and Japanese gardens, pots and in combination with blue or green grasses.
94.planting: It reaches 30–50 cm. Plant 7–9 plants per square metre for mass planting. It prefers sun or partial shade – the colour is more intense in sun – and moist, well-drained soils.
94.care: In late autumn or at the end of winter cut the dry leaves back close to the ground. In regions with harsh winters mulch the base. The 'Red Baron' variety spreads slowly, unlike the wild species. Hardy to about -20°C.

faq.q: When does Japanese blood grass colour up?
faq.a: The leaves turn red gradually from spring, with the most intense colour in autumn.

faq.q: Does 'Red Baron' spread?
faq.a: Very slowly; 'Red Baron' does not spread aggressively like the wild species.

95.uses: Thanks to its moderate size and compact crown, trident maple is chosen for narrow streets, urban squares, car parks and residential gardens. It tolerates heat and urban conditions well and gives warm orange and red autumn colour.
95.planting: It reaches 8–10 m with a rounded crown. In avenues it is planted 6–8 m apart. It prefers sun and well-drained soils and tolerates short dry spells once established.
95.care: Water regularly for the first two years after planting. Formative pruning is done in winter or late summer. It is hardy to about -20°C.

faq.q: How big does trident maple grow?
faq.a: Usually 8–10 m, with a compact rounded crown – suitable for streets and small spaces.

faq.q: Is it suitable for urban planting?
faq.a: Yes, it tolerates heat, compacted soils and urban conditions well.

96.uses: Field maple is one of the most robust trees for urban planting: street avenues, parks, car parks and shelter belts. Narrow or oval-crowned cultivars such as 'Elsrijk', 'Lienco' and 'Huibers Elegant' are selected for streets, and the species is also used for clipped hedges.
96.planting: It reaches 10–15 m depending on the cultivar. In avenues it is planted 6–10 m apart. It grows in almost any soil, including chalky, dry or clay soils, in sun or partial shade.
96.care: Low maintenance: water during the first years and carry out formative pruning in winter. It tolerates pruning, pollution and drought very well. Hardy to about -30°C.

faq.q: Which field maple cultivars suit street planting?
faq.a: Compact-crowned cultivars such as 'Elsrijk', 'Lienco', 'Huibers Elegant' and 'Green Column' are selected specifically for avenues.

faq.q: Is field maple drought tolerant?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the most drought-tolerant trees and copes well with chalky soils.

97.uses: It combines the fast growth of silver maple with the autumn colour of red maple, which makes it very popular for avenues, parks and residential developments. 'Autumn Blaze' has an oval crown and intense red-orange colour, 'Armstrong' is columnar for narrow streets, and 'Celebration' has a regular, well-structured crown.
97.planting: It reaches 12–15 m ('Armstrong' stays narrow, about 4–5 m wide). In avenues plant 7–10 m apart ('Armstrong' 5–6 m). It tolerates various soils, including moist ones, in sun or partial shade.
97.care: Water regularly during the first years. Formative pruning in late summer or winter to avoid sap bleeding in spring. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: What is the difference between 'Autumn Blaze' and 'Armstrong'?
faq.a: 'Autumn Blaze' has a broad oval crown and the most intense autumn colour; 'Armstrong' has a narrow columnar crown for streets and tight spaces.

faq.q: How fast does it grow?
faq.a: Fast – it is one of the quickest-growing maples for urban planting.

98.uses: 'Flamingo' is chosen for its colour effect: pink young foliage turning white and green brightens gardens, entrances and groups of darker shrubs. It is used as a standard specimen tree in residential gardens, small parks and courtyards.
98.planting: It reaches 5–7 m with a rounded crown. Plant as a specimen or in small groups, 4–5 m apart. Colour is best in sun or bright partial shade.
98.care: Light pruning in late winter encourages new, most colourful shoots. Remove any branches reverting to plain green leaves. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Why are the shoots pink?
faq.a: On 'Flamingo' young leaves emerge pink in spring and then turn white and green; light pruning encourages new coloured shoots.

faq.q: How big does it get?
faq.a: It is a small tree of 5–7 m, also suitable for smaller gardens.

99.uses: These are modern avenue trees of medium size with regular crowns, suitable for streets, car parks, squares and residential developments. 'Pacific Sunset' has a rounded-oval crown and early yellow-orange-red autumn colour; 'Norwegian Sunset' has a narrower oval crown.
99.planting: They reach 9–11 m tall and 7–8 m wide ('Norwegian Sunset' narrower). In avenues plant 7–9 m apart. They tolerate various soils, heat and moderate drought.
99.care: Regular watering for the first two years. Formative pruning in late summer or winter. Very frost hardy and tolerant of urban conditions.

faq.q: What do 'Warrenred' and 'Keithsform' mean?
faq.a: They are the official cultivar names: 'Pacific Sunset' = 'Warrenred', 'Norwegian Sunset' = 'Keithsform'.

faq.q: Are they suitable for streets?
faq.a: Yes, they are of moderate size with a regular crown and were selected specifically for avenue planting.

100.uses: Sycamore gives dense shade and an imposing silhouette in parks, squares and wide avenues. 'Atropurpureum' has leaves green above and purple beneath, decorative in the wind, while 'Bruchem' has a narrower oval crown suitable for streets.
100.planting: It reaches 20–30 m with a broad crown ('Bruchem' narrower). In avenues plant 10–12 m apart. It grows well on fertile soils, including chalky ones, and tolerates exposed, windy sites.
100.care: Water during the first years after planting and carry out formative pruning in winter. Very hardy to frost and wind. Not recommended for very tight spaces because of its size.

faq.q: How big does sycamore maple grow?
faq.a: It is a large tree of 20–30 m; for streets choose narrower cultivars such as 'Bruchem'.

faq.q: What does 'Atropurpureum' look like?
faq.a: Its leaves are dark green above and purple underneath, giving a two-tone effect in the wind.

101.uses: A small tree or large shrub valued for its intense red autumn colour and its tolerance of cold and drought. It is used in small gardens, parks, shelter belts, informal hedges and as a standard tree in tight spaces.
101.planting: It reaches 5–7 m. Plant as a specimen, in groups 3–4 m apart or in hedges 1–1.5 m apart. It grows in most soils, ideally in sun for the best colour.
101.care: Very low maintenance and tolerant of pruning. Extremely frost hardy (to about -35°C) and drought tolerant once established.

faq.q: When does Amur maple colour up?
faq.a: In autumn the leaves turn bright red, sometimes orange – one of the most intense autumn colours.

faq.q: Can it be used for hedging?
faq.a: Yes, it tolerates pruning well and forms dense informal or clipped hedges.

102.uses: The hybrid 'Annae' (related to field maple) is valued for its coloured young foliage and its toughness. It is used in avenues, parks and public spaces where it brings a subtle colour contrast in spring.
102.planting: It reaches 10–12 m with a compact oval crown. In avenues plant 7–9 m apart. It tolerates various soils and urban conditions.
102.care: Water during the first years and prune for form in winter. Hardy to frost and pollution, with low maintenance needs.

faq.q: Which tree is 'Annae' similar to?
faq.a: It is a hybrid related to field maple, just as tough but with red-violet young foliage.

faq.q: Is it suitable for avenues?
faq.a: Yes, it has a compact crown and copes well with urban conditions.

103.uses: Unlike other alders, Italian alder also tolerates dry and chalky soils, so it is used in avenues, car parks, shelter belts and industrial areas. The glossy foliage stays green until late autumn.
103.planting: It reaches 15–20 m with a regular conical crown. In avenues plant 7–10 m apart. It fixes nitrogen from the air, which helps it on poor soils.
103.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. It grows fast and responds well to formative pruning. Hardy to about -20°C.

faq.q: Does Italian alder tolerate drought?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the few alders that grows well on drier and chalky soils.

faq.q: How fast does it grow?
faq.a: Fast – it is used when a quick effect is needed in avenues and shelter belts.

104.uses: Common alder is the classic choice for waterside planting, wetlands, retention basins and bank stabilisation. The finely cut-leaved cultivars 'Imperialis' and 'Laciniata' are elegant ornamental trees for parks and large gardens.
104.planting: The species reaches 15–25 m; the ornamental cultivars stay smaller. Plant 6–10 m apart, or closer in screens. It prefers moist soils, even temporarily flooded, and fixes nitrogen from the air.
104.care: On moist soils it needs very little maintenance. It tolerates pruning and regenerates well. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Where is common alder planted?
faq.a: Along watercourses, in wetlands, next to retention basins and on soils that may be temporarily flooded.

faq.q: Which ornamental cultivars are there?
faq.a: 'Imperialis' and 'Laciniata' have deeply cut, fine-looking leaves and suit parks.

105.uses: It is one of the best alders for towns: it tolerates compacted soils, heat and pollution. It is used in avenues, car parks, industrial areas and parks, where the foliage stays green and healthy until late autumn.
105.planting: It reaches 15–20 m with a regular oval crown. In avenues plant 7–10 m apart. It grows on moist as well as drier soils.
105.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Fast-growing and tolerant of pruning. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Why is Spaeth's alder good for towns?
faq.a: It tolerates compacted soils, heat and pollution better than common alder.

faq.q: What are the leaves like?
faq.a: Large, elongated and glossy, with purplish tints on the young shoots.

106.uses: It offers interest in every season: abundant blossom in April, berries loved by birds, bronze new leaves and spectacular autumn colour. Standard forms suit narrow streets, courtyards, residential gardens and small spaces.
106.planting: It reaches 5–8 m with an oval crown ('Robin Hill' narrower). Plant 4–6 m apart. It prefers well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soils in sun or partial shade.
106.care: Low maintenance and almost no pruning needed. Water during the first years after planting. Very frost hardy (to about -30°C).

faq.q: When does amelanchier flower?
faq.a: In April, before or as the leaves emerge, with masses of white flowers.

faq.q: Are the berries edible?
faq.a: Yes, the small dark berries are edible and very popular with birds.

107.uses: It is chosen mainly for its coloured bark, especially visible in winter. Plant as a specimen or in small groups in parks, residential gardens, office courtyards and modern landscape schemes.
107.planting: It reaches 12–15 m with an oval crown. Plant 5–8 m apart or in groups. It prefers moist but well-drained soils in sun or partial shade.
107.care: Water regularly during the first years, especially in summer. Prune only in late summer, as birches bleed a lot of sap in spring. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: What makes 'Fascination' special?
faq.a: Its peeling orange-copper bark with pink and cream tones – most decorative in winter.

faq.q: When should birch be pruned?
faq.a: In late summer; in spring birches lose a lot of sap when cut.

108.uses: It is one of the few birches that tolerate both wet soils and summer heat. It is used in parks, along watercourses, in rain gardens and as a specimen, often multi-stemmed, for its bark.
108.planting: It reaches 12–18 m with an oval crown. Plant 6–8 m apart. It prefers moist, slightly acidic soils; on very chalky soils the leaves may yellow.
108.care: Water regularly, especially in dry spells. Prune in late summer. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Does river birch tolerate wet soils?
faq.a: Yes, it grows well on moist and even temporarily flooded soils, for example along watercourses.

faq.q: Why is its bark valued?
faq.a: It peels in thin layers in cinnamon and pinkish-brown tones and is decorative all year.

109.uses: Unlike silver birch, downy birch tolerates wet, cold soils. It is used in naturalistic parks, afforestation, wetlands and group planting, where the white bark and light foliage create a bright effect.
109.planting: It reaches 15–20 m with an airy oval crown. Plant in groups or 5–8 m apart. It prefers moist, acidic to neutral soils.
109.care: Low maintenance. Prune only in late summer. Extremely frost hardy.

faq.q: How does it differ from silver birch?
faq.a: Its young shoots are downy and it copes better with wet, cold soils.

faq.q: Where is it used?
faq.a: In naturalistic parks, afforestation, wetlands and group planting.

110.uses: 'Doorenbos' (syn. jacquemontii) is chosen for its snow-white peeling bark, which stays clean and bright. It is planted as a specimen, in groups or multi-stemmed in residential gardens, office courtyards, hotels and urban squares.
110.planting: It reaches 12–15 m with an airy oval crown. Plant 5–7 m apart or in groups of 3–5. It prefers moist, well-drained soils in sun or partial shade.
110.care: Water regularly in the first years. Prune in late summer. The bark can be gently washed for maximum effect. Hardy to about -30°C.

faq.q: Why is the bark so white?
faq.a: 'Doorenbos' was selected for its pure white peeling bark, which stays bright all year.

faq.q: Can it be planted in groups?
faq.a: Yes, groups of 3–5 trees or multi-stemmed forms are very decorative.

111.uses: Hornbeam is one of the most versatile trees: it is used in avenues, parks, shelter belts, pleached or roof-trained trees and tall hedges. It tolerates shade, clay soils and urban conditions.
111.planting: Free-growing it reaches 15–20 m. In avenues plant 6–8 m apart; for hedges, 30–50 cm apart. It grows on almost all soils, from sandy to clay, in sun or shade.
111.care: It tolerates pruning very well, done in summer (June–August) for compact shapes. Water during the first years. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: What are standard hornbeams used for?
faq.a: For avenues, trained trees (pleached, roof-shaped) and tall green screens in urban spaces.

faq.q: Does hornbeam tolerate shade?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the few trees that grows well in partial or full shade.

112.uses: A small ornamental tree valued for its finely pleated leaves and hanging fruit clusters, green then brown. It is used as a specimen in residential gardens, courtyards, Japanese gardens and parks.
112.planting: It reaches 8–10 m with a broad, layered crown. Plant as a specimen or 5–6 m apart. It prefers fertile, well-drained soils in sun or partial shade.
112.care: Low maintenance with minimal pruning. Water during the first years. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: How big does Japanese hornbeam grow?
faq.a: Usually 8–10 m with a broad crown – suitable for smaller gardens.

faq.q: What makes it ornamental?
faq.a: Its closely veined, pleated leaves and hanging hop-like fruits.

113.uses: Sweet chestnut is an imposing park tree with fragrant summer flowers and edible chestnuts in autumn. It is used in parks, estates, wide avenues and orchards, especially in areas with acidic soils and mild climate.
113.planting: It reaches 20–30 m with a broad crown. Plant 10–12 m apart. It prefers acidic to neutral, well-drained soils and does not tolerate very chalky soils.
113.care: Water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. For a good crop plant at least two trees for pollination. Hardy to about -20°C.

faq.q: Which soil does sweet chestnut prefer?
faq.a: Acidic to neutral, well-drained soils; it grows poorly on chalky soils.

faq.q: Are two trees needed for chestnuts?
faq.a: Yes, planting at least two trees is recommended for good fruiting.

114.uses: Celtis is increasingly used in towns as an alternative to elm and plane because of its resistance to drought, heat and pollution. It is planted in avenues, squares, car parks and parks. C. australis suits warm regions, C. occidentalis colder climates.
114.planting: It reaches 15–20 m with a broad, rounded crown. In avenues plant 8–10 m apart. It grows on almost all soils, including poor, chalky and dry ones.
114.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. C. occidentalis is very frost hardy, C. australis to about -20°C.

faq.q: What is the difference between C. australis and C. occidentalis?
faq.a: C. australis (Mediterranean) prefers warm regions; C. occidentalis (American) is hardier to frost.

faq.q: Why is it used in towns?
faq.a: It copes very well with drought, heat, compacted soils and pollution.

115.uses: Katsura is valued for its delicate foliage, reddish when emerging and yellow-orange-pink in autumn, and for the caramel scent of fallen leaves. It is planted as a specimen in parks, residential gardens and Japanese gardens.
115.planting: It reaches 10–15 m with a pyramidal crown that later broadens. Plant as a specimen or 6–8 m apart. It prefers moist, well-drained soils and a site sheltered from drying winds.
115.care: It needs regular watering, especially in dry summers when the leaves can suffer. Pruning is rarely necessary. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Why does it smell of caramel?
faq.a: In autumn the fallen leaves release an aromatic compound that smells of caramel and gingerbread.

faq.q: Does it need a lot of water?
faq.a: Yes, it prefers moist soils and should be watered regularly in dry summers.

116.uses: A small tree, very decorative in spring, suitable for residential gardens, courtyards, parks and narrow street avenues. The large heart-shaped leaves give elegant summer foliage and turn yellow in autumn.
116.planting: It reaches 6–9 m with a broad, rounded crown. Plant 5–6 m apart. It prefers well-drained soils in sun or partial shade.
116.care: It does not like being moved when older, so correct planting from the start is important. Water during the first years. Minimal pruning, after flowering. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: When does eastern redbud flower?
faq.a: In April, before the leaves, with pink-purple flowers directly on branches and trunk.

faq.q: How does it differ from Cercis siliquastrum?
faq.a: Its leaves are thinner and pointed, and it is hardier than the Mediterranean species.

117.uses: Turkish hazel is an excellent avenue tree: a symmetrical crown, deep roots that do not lift paving and high tolerance of drought, heat and road salt. It is used on streets, boulevards, car parks and urban squares.
117.planting: It reaches 15–20 m with a regular conical crown. In avenues plant 7–9 m apart. It grows in almost any soil, including chalky and dry ones.
117.care: Very low maintenance and hardly any formative pruning needed thanks to its naturally regular crown. Water during the first years. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Why is it good for avenues?
faq.a: It has a naturally regular crown and deep roots, and tolerates drought, heat and road salt.

faq.q: Does it produce nuts?
faq.a: Yes, small edible hazelnuts in fringed husks, but it is grown mainly as an ornamental tree.

118.uses: Standard hawthorn is an ideal small tree for narrow streets, squares, car parks and gardens thanks to its compact size and resistance to drought, wind and pollution. 'Paul's Scarlet' has double carmine-red flowers, 'Carrierei' glossy foliage and long-lasting orange fruits, and 'Splendens' is a robust cultivar with a regular crown.
118.planting: It reaches 5–8 m with a rounded crown. In avenues plant 5–7 m apart. It grows in almost any soil, including chalky and dry ones, preferably in sun.
118.care: Very low maintenance; it tolerates pruning well, done after flowering or in winter. Water during the first years. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: When does 'Paul's Scarlet' flower?
faq.a: In May, with masses of double carmine-red flowers.

faq.q: Is it suitable for narrow streets?
faq.a: Yes, it stays small (5–8 m) and copes well with urban conditions.

119.uses: It is one of the most spectacular flowering trees: large white bracts cover the crown in late spring. It is planted as a specimen in parks, large gardens, estates, hotels and arboreta, where it attracts attention.
119.planting: It reaches 10–15 m with a pyramidal crown that later broadens. Plant as a specimen with plenty of space. It prefers fertile, moist but well-drained soils and a site sheltered from wind.
119.care: Water regularly, especially in summer. It usually starts flowering a few years after planting. Pruning is rarely necessary. Hardy to about -20°C.

faq.q: When do the white 'handkerchiefs' appear?
faq.a: In May, when the large white bracts hang from the branches around the flowers.

faq.q: Does it flower straight after planting?
faq.a: It usually flowers after a few years, once the tree matures.

120.uses: Beech is one of the noblest park trees: the green species and the copper beech ('Atropunicea') are imposing specimens, the columnar 'Dawyck' (green) and 'Dawyck Purple' fit narrow spaces, and 'Purpurea Pendula' is a small weeping tree for gardens. Beech is also used for tall hedges.
120.planting: The species reaches 25–30 m; the columnar cultivars stay narrow (2–3 m wide). Plant in fertile, well-drained soils without waterlogging. It does not tolerate compacted or waterlogged soils.
120.care: Water regularly in the first years; beech needs time to establish. The thin bark is sensitive to sunscald – protect young trunks. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Which beech suits narrow spaces?
faq.a: The columnar cultivars 'Dawyck' (green) and 'Dawyck Purple', which stay narrow.

faq.q: Does beech tolerate wet soils?
faq.a: No, it prefers well-drained soils; waterlogging and compaction harm it.

121.uses: Selected white ash cultivars are valued avenue trees with symmetrical crowns and autumn colour: 'Autumn Purple' and 'Autumn Applause' turn purple-burgundy, while 'Skyline' has a compact oval crown suitable for streets.
121.planting: It reaches 15–20 m. In avenues plant 8–10 m apart. It tolerates various soils, ideally fertile and well-drained, in sun.
121.care: Water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Hardy to about -30°C.

faq.q: What colour is white ash in autumn?
faq.a: 'Autumn Purple' and 'Autumn Applause' turn purple-burgundy, a rare colour among trees.

faq.q: Which cultivar suits streets?
faq.a: 'Skyline' has a compact, regular oval crown suitable for avenues.

122.uses: 'Raywood' is valued for its fine foliage, giving light shade, and its claret autumn colour. It tolerates drought and heat well and suits avenues, car parks and parks in areas with hot summers.
122.planting: It reaches 12–15 m with a compact oval crown. In avenues plant 7–9 m apart. It grows on various soils, including chalky and dry ones.
122.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: What colour is 'Raywood' in autumn?
faq.a: The leaves turn claret-purple, hence its popular name 'claret ash'.

faq.q: Is it drought tolerant?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the most drought- and heat-tolerant ashes.

123.uses: European ash gives light, dappled shade in parks, wide avenues and natural landscapes. The cultivars 'Altena' and 'Atlas' have regular crowns suitable for streets, while 'Jaspidea' is decorative in winter thanks to its golden-yellow shoots.
123.planting: It reaches 20–30 m. In avenues plant 10–12 m apart. It prefers fertile, deep, moist but well-drained soils, including chalky ones.
123.care: Water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Which cultivar has yellow twigs?
faq.a: 'Jaspidea' has golden-yellow shoots, decorative in winter, and yellow autumn leaves.

faq.q: Which cultivars suit avenues?
faq.a: 'Altena' and 'Atlas', which have regular, compact crowns.

124.uses: 'Summit' is an avenue cultivar with a regular oval-pyramidal crown that needs little formative pruning. It is used on streets, boulevards, car parks and industrial areas, where it copes with difficult conditions.
124.planting: It reaches 12–15 m. In avenues plant 7–9 m apart. It tolerates poor, wet or dry soils and road salt.
124.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Minimal formative pruning in winter. Extremely frost hardy.

faq.q: What colour is 'Summit' in autumn?
faq.a: The leaves turn golden yellow.

faq.q: Why is it used on streets?
faq.a: It has a naturally regular crown and tolerates difficult soils, drought and salt.

125.uses: Ginkgo is one of the toughest urban trees: it tolerates pollution, heat and compacted soils and is practically free of pests and diseases. It is planted in avenues, squares, courtyards, parks and as a specimen for its spectacular golden autumn colour.
125.planting: It grows slowly at first and reaches 15–25 m, with an initially narrow crown. In avenues plant 8–10 m apart. It tolerates almost any well-drained soil.
125.care: Very low maintenance and hardly any pruning. Water during the first years. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Why is ginkgo good for towns?
faq.a: It tolerates pollution, heat and compacted soils and is practically free of pests and diseases.

faq.q: When do the leaves change colour?
faq.a: In autumn the leaves turn intense golden yellow and fall almost at the same time.

126.uses: Thornless honey locust is a valued avenue tree for its light shade, which lets lawn grow beneath the crown, and its tolerance of drought, heat and salt. 'Rubylace' has ruby-red young leaves, while the inermis form is green and vigorous.
126.planting: It reaches 12–20 m depending on the cultivar, with a broad airy crown. In avenues plant 8–10 m apart. It grows in almost any soil, including poor and dry ones.
126.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning in late summer. Hardy to about -30°C.

faq.q: Do these cultivars have thorns?
faq.a: No, all forms offered (inermis, 'Rubylace', 'Speczam') are thornless.

faq.q: Why does grass grow under honey locust?
faq.a: The fine pinnate foliage lets plenty of light through, giving light shade.

127.uses: Black walnut is an imposing park tree with a broad crown and elegant foliage, and a valuable species for quality timber plantations. It is planted in large parks, estates, forest belts and plantations.
127.planting: It reaches 20–30 m with a broad crown. Plant 10–12 m apart. It prefers deep, fertile, well-drained soils in sun.
127.care: Water during the first years. Prune in late summer, as walnuts bleed sap in spring. The roots release substances that can inhibit some nearby plants. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Are black walnuts edible?
faq.a: Yes, with an intense flavour, but the shell is very hard; the tree is grown mainly for timber and as a park tree.

faq.q: Anything to know about planting near other plants?
faq.a: Black walnut releases juglone, which can inhibit the growth of some sensitive plants nearby.

128.uses: Walnut is the classic tree for large yards, farms, orchards and parks, providing dense shade and nuts. It is also used in timber plantations and wide rural avenues.
128.planting: It reaches 15–25 m with a broad, rounded crown. Plant 10–12 m apart. It prefers deep, fertile, well-drained soils in sunny sites protected from late frosts.
128.care: Water during the first years. Prune in summer or late summer, not spring, to avoid sap bleeding. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: When should walnut be pruned?
faq.a: In summer or late summer; in spring walnut bleeds a lot of sap when cut.

faq.q: How big does walnut get?
faq.a: It is a large tree of 15–25 m with a broad crown – it needs space.

129.uses: It is one of the few trees that flower in high summer (July), with golden-yellow flowers followed by pinkish-brown lantern fruits. It tolerates drought, heat and pollution well and suits urban squares, streets, car parks, courtyards and residential gardens.
129.planting: It reaches 8–12 m with a broad, rounded crown. Plant 6–8 m apart. It grows in almost any well-drained soil, including chalky ones, in sun.
129.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: When does it flower?
faq.a: In July, with large panicles of golden-yellow flowers – a time when few trees bloom.

faq.q: Is it suitable for hot, dry areas?
faq.a: Yes, it copes very well with drought, heat and chalky soils.

130.uses: Japanese larch is valued for its fast growth and golden autumn colour, rare among conifers. It is used in parks, afforestation, shelter belts and large gardens, as a specimen or in groups.
130.planting: It reaches 20–30 m with a conical crown. Plant 5–8 m apart or in groups. It prefers moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soils in full sun.
130.care: Water during the first years. No pruning needed. Extremely frost hardy (to about -35°C).

faq.q: Does larch lose its needles in winter?
faq.a: Yes, larch is a deciduous conifer: the needles turn golden and fall in autumn and regrow in spring.

faq.q: How does it differ from European larch?
faq.a: Japanese larch has bluer needles, reddish shoots and grows faster.

131.uses: It is one of the hardiest magnolias, also suitable for colder areas. It is planted as a specimen or standard in parks, residential gardens, courtyards and pedestrian avenues, where the white spring blossom is spectacular.
131.planting: It reaches 8–12 m with a rounded or pyramidal crown. Plant 6–8 m apart. It prefers fertile, slightly acidic to neutral, well-drained soils in sun or partial shade.
131.care: Water regularly during the first years. Prune only if needed, after flowering. Young trees start flowering after a few years. Hardy to about -30°C.

faq.q: When does Magnolia kobus flower?
faq.a: In April, before the leaves, with many fragrant white flowers.

faq.q: Is it frost hardy?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the hardiest magnolias, to about -30°C.

132.uses: 'Susan' belongs to the 'Little Girl' hybrid series, compact and free-flowering, sometimes with a second flush in summer. It is ideal for residential gardens, courtyards, entrances and small spaces, as a specimen or standard.
132.planting: It reaches 3–5 m with a compact crown. Plant 3–4 m apart. It prefers fertile, slightly acidic, well-drained soils in sun or partial shade.
132.care: Water regularly, especially in the first years and in dry summers. Minimal pruning, after flowering. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Why does it flower later?
faq.a: 'Susan' flowers in April–May, after most magnolias, so the flowers are rarely damaged by late frosts.

faq.q: Is it suitable for small gardens?
faq.a: Yes, it stays small (3–5 m) and compact.

133.uses: Standard apple trees combine ornamental value – white-pink spring blossom – with fruit production. They are planted in traditional orchards, residential gardens, community gardens, schools and parks. 'Elstar' is an aromatic dessert apple, 'Gravensteiner' an old fragrant variety and 'Glorie van Holland' a traditional Dutch cultivar.
133.planting: Standard trees reach 5–8 m. Plant 6–8 m apart. They prefer fertile, well-drained soils in sun. Plant several cultivars for pollination.
133.care: Formative and fruiting pruning in late winter. Water during the first years and in dry spells. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Do several cultivars need to be planted?
faq.a: Yes, most apple cultivars need another cultivar nearby for good pollination.

faq.q: What is a standard fruit tree?
faq.a: A tree with a straight, clear stem of about 1.8–2 m and the crown above – suitable for traditional orchards and public spaces.

134.uses: Known as a 'living fossil', dawn redwood is a spectacular tree with a regular conical silhouette and copper autumn colour. It is planted as a specimen or in groups in parks, by water, in wet areas and in wide avenues.
134.planting: It grows fast and reaches 25–35 m with a narrow conical crown. Plant 6–8 m apart. It prefers moist, fertile soils and tolerates temporarily flooded soils.
134.care: Water regularly, especially in dry summers. No pruning needed. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Does it lose its needles in winter?
faq.a: Yes, dawn redwood is a deciduous conifer; in autumn the needles turn copper and fall.

faq.q: Where does it grow best?
faq.a: In sunny sites with moist soil – for example in parks, by lakes or rivers.

135.uses: Mulberry is a traditional shade tree for yards, squares, terraces and car parks. The 'Fruitless' cultivar is preferred over paving because it does not stain the ground. The fruiting species is planted in yards and orchards.
135.planting: It reaches 8–15 m with a broad, rounded crown. Plant 6–8 m apart. It grows in almost any soil, including poor and dry ones, in sun.
135.care: It tolerates pruning very well, including training as umbrella or roof shapes. Water during the first years. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: What does 'Fruitless' mean?
faq.a: It is a male cultivar without fruit, so it does not stain paving – suitable for squares, terraces and car parks.

faq.q: Is it drought tolerant?
faq.a: Yes, white mulberry copes very well with drought and heat once established.

136.uses: Native to southern Europe, hop hornbeam is increasingly used in towns thanks to its resistance to drought and heat. It is planted in avenues, car parks, parks and on chalky ground where other species struggle.
136.planting: It reaches 12–15 m with a conical, later rounded crown. In avenues plant 7–9 m apart. It grows well on chalky, dry and stony soils.
136.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Is it suitable for dry areas?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the most drought-, heat- and lime-tolerant species.

faq.q: What do the fruits look like?
faq.a: They are grouped in hanging, hop-like clusters.

137.uses: A small to medium-sized tree, decorative in every season: tiny red winter flowers, healthy summer foliage, spectacular autumn colour and mottled bark. The species has a broad crown, while 'Vanessa' is narrow, suitable for streets and small spaces.
137.planting: It reaches 6–10 m ('Vanessa' narrower). Plant 5–7 m apart. It tolerates various well-drained soils, including chalky ones, in sun or partial shade.
137.care: Low maintenance with little pruning. Water during the first years. Hardy to about -25°C and very healthy.

faq.q: Which cultivar suits streets?
faq.a: 'Vanessa', with its upright, narrower crown.

faq.q: When is it most decorative?
faq.a: In autumn, when the leaves turn yellow, orange and red, often on the same tree.

138.uses: A tree with character, valued for its thick, furrowed bark and broad, airy crown. It is planted as a specimen or in groups in parks, squares and wide avenues.
138.planting: It reaches 10–15 m with a broad crown. Plant 8–10 m apart. It tolerates almost any soil, including dry and chalky ones, in sun.
138.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Extremely frost hardy.

faq.q: Why is it called a cork tree?
faq.a: Its bark is thick, soft and furrowed, like cork.

faq.q: Is it suitable for towns?
faq.a: Yes, it tolerates drought, heat and urban conditions.

139.uses: 'Robusta' is a male hybrid poplar (no fluffy seed), used for a quick effect: windbreaks, avenues along roads and canals, industrial areas and large green spaces.
139.planting: It grows very fast and reaches 25–30 m. Plant 6–10 m apart. It tolerates various soils, preferably moist. Do not plant close to buildings and pipes because of its vigorous roots.
139.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Does 'Robusta' produce fluff?
faq.a: No, it is a male clone, so it does not produce the seed fluff of female poplars.

faq.q: Where is it not recommended?
faq.a: Near buildings, pipes and paving, because of its size and vigorous roots.

140.uses: The species is used in naturalistic planting, afforestation and shelter belts. 'Erecta' is an elegant columnar tree for narrow streets, vertical accents in parks and modern gardens.
140.planting: The species reaches 15–20 m; 'Erecta' stays narrow, 1.5–2 m wide. Plant 'Erecta' 2–4 m apart in rows. It tolerates almost any soil.
140.care: Very low maintenance and fast growth. Water during the first years. Extremely frost hardy.

faq.q: Why do the leaves tremble?
faq.a: The long, flattened leaf stalks make the leaves move in the slightest breeze.

faq.q: How narrow does 'Erecta' stay?
faq.a: Only about 1.5–2 m wide, so it suits narrow spaces.

141.uses: The fruiting cultivars are planted in orchards, yards, community gardens and schools. 'Plena' is a valued ornamental tree for avenues and parks: abundant double white blossom in April and no fruit to stain the paving.
141.planting: Standard cherries reach 8–15 m. Plant 7–10 m apart. They prefer fertile, well-drained soils in sun. 'Lapins' and 'Stella' are self-fertile; the other cultivars need pollinators.
141.care: Prune in summer after harvest to reduce disease risk. Water during the first years. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Which cultivars are self-fertile?
faq.a: 'Lapins' and 'Stella' are self-fertile; 'Kordia', 'Regina', 'Van' and 'Hedelfinger' need another cultivar for pollination.

faq.q: Does 'Plena' produce cherries?
faq.a: No, 'Plena' has sterile double flowers and is purely ornamental.

142.uses: Standard plum trees are planted in traditional orchards, yards, residential gardens and school or community gardens. 'Opal' ripens early, in mid-summer, while 'Victoria' is a popular cultivar with large red fruit.
142.planting: They reach 5–7 m. Plant 5–6 m apart. They prefer fertile, well-drained soils in sun. Both cultivars are self-fertile.
142.care: Prune in summer to reduce disease risk. Thin the fruit in heavy years to prevent branches breaking. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Are 'Opal' and 'Victoria' self-fertile?
faq.a: Yes, both are self-fertile and crop without another cultivar nearby.

faq.q: When should plum be pruned?
faq.a: In summer after harvest; winter pruning increases the risk of disease.

143.uses: Bird cherry is valued for its fragrant blossom and for fruit that attracts birds. It is used in parks, naturalistic planting, along watercourses and in avenues. 'Watereri' has very long flower racemes, while 'Tiefurt' has a regular crown suitable for streets.
143.planting: It reaches 10–15 m. Plant 6–8 m apart. It prefers moist, fertile soils but tolerates various soils, in sun or partial shade.
143.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning after flowering or in winter. Extremely frost hardy.

faq.q: When does bird cherry flower?
faq.a: In May, with long racemes of strongly scented white flowers.

faq.q: Which cultivar suits streets?
faq.a: 'Tiefurt', which has a compact, regular crown.

144.uses: 'Canada Red' brings purple colour to avenues, car parks, residential gardens and parks, contrasting well with green trees. It stays small and is very tolerant of cold and drought.
144.planting: It reaches 6–8 m with an oval-rounded crown. Plant 5–6 m apart. It tolerates almost any well-drained soil; colour is most intense in sun.
144.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Remove suckers from the base. Extremely frost hardy.

faq.q: When do the leaves turn purple?
faq.a: They emerge green in spring and turn dark purple-red in early summer.

faq.q: How big does it get?
faq.a: It is a small tree of 6–8 m, suitable for streets and gardens.

145.uses: An imposing exotic tree, decorative in summer thanks to green fruit strings up to 40–50 cm long. It is planted as a specimen in large parks, estates and along lakes and rivers.
145.planting: It reaches 20–25 m with a very broad crown, often multi-stemmed. It needs a lot of space. It prefers moist, fertile soils, even temporarily flooded.
145.care: Water regularly on drier soils. Remove basal suckers if a single trunk is wanted. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Where is it best planted?
faq.a: By water or on moist soils in large parks, where it has room for its broad crown.

faq.q: What are the long strings?
faq.a: Small winged fruits in hanging strings 40–50 cm long, decorative in summer.

146.uses: Standard pears are long-lived trees with white spring blossom and autumn fruit, suitable for traditional orchards, yards, community gardens and parks. 'Conference' is one of Europe's most widely grown dessert pears, while 'Saint Rémy' and 'Zoete Brederode' are traditional cultivars.
146.planting: They reach 8–12 m. Plant 7–9 m apart. They prefer fertile, deep, well-drained soils in sun. Plant several cultivars for good fruiting.
146.care: Formative and fruiting pruning in late winter. Water during the first years. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Is 'Conference' self-fertile?
faq.a: It is partly self-fertile but crops better with another pear cultivar nearby.

faq.q: How long does a standard pear live?
faq.a: Standard pears are very long-lived and can live and crop for many decades.

147.uses: 'Chanticleer' is a very popular avenue tree in Europe: a narrow conical crown, spectacular spring blossom, glossy summer foliage and late autumn colour. It tolerates pollution, drought and compacted soils.
147.planting: It reaches 10–12 m tall and only 4–5 m wide. In avenues plant 5–7 m apart. It grows in almost any soil, in sun.
147.care: Low maintenance; hardly any pruning needed thanks to its regular crown. Water during the first years. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Does it produce edible fruit?
faq.a: No, the fruits are tiny and of no value; the tree is purely ornamental.

faq.q: How wide is the crown?
faq.a: Only 4–5 m, which makes it ideal for narrow streets.

148.uses: One of the most elegant small garden trees: the silvery weeping crown contrasts beautifully with green or purple plants. It is used as a standard specimen in residential gardens, courtyards, cemeteries, Mediterranean gardens and at entrances.
148.planting: It reaches 4–6 m with a rounded weeping crown. Plant as a specimen, 3–5 m from other plants. It prefers well-drained soils in full sun and tolerates drought.
148.care: The crown can be thinned or lightly shaped in winter. Water during the first years. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: How tall are the trees?
faq.a: The tree stays small (4–5 m); the clear stem height is shown for each size (e.g. 180–250 cm).

faq.q: Is it drought tolerant?
faq.a: Yes, its silver leaves are adapted to sunny, dry sites.

149.uses: Turkey oak is one of the most drought- and heat-tolerant oaks, a good choice for an increasingly warm climate. It is planted in parks, wide avenues, shelter belts and afforestation.
149.planting: It reaches 20–30 m with a broad crown. Plant 10–12 m apart. It grows in almost any soil, including chalky and dry ones.
149.care: Water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Does Turkey oak grow fast?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the fastest-growing oaks.

faq.q: Why is it recommended for warm areas?
faq.a: It tolerates drought, heat and chalky soils very well.

150.uses: One of the toughest oaks: it tolerates drought, extreme cold, heavy soils and urban conditions. It is planted in parks, wide avenues and large green spaces, where it develops a broad, imposing crown over time.
150.planting: It reaches 20–25 m with a broad crown. Plant 10–12 m apart. It grows in almost any soil, including clay and chalky ones.
150.care: Water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Extremely frost hardy (to about -35°C).

faq.q: Why is it valued?
faq.a: For its exceptional resistance to drought, frost and urban conditions, and its large leaves and acorns.

faq.q: What do the acorns look like?
faq.a: They are large, with a fringed cup covering much of the acorn.

151.uses: A highly valued avenue oak thanks to its regular pyramidal crown and red autumn colour. It is planted on wide streets, boulevards, in parks and as a specimen, and also tolerates moist soils.
151.planting: It reaches 15–20 m with a conical crown. In avenues plant 8–10 m apart. It prefers acidic to neutral soils; on chalky soils the leaves may yellow.
151.care: Water during the first years. The drooping lower branches are gradually removed for avenue use. Hardy to about -30°C.

faq.q: When does pin oak colour up?
faq.a: In autumn the leaves turn bright red to burgundy.

faq.q: Which soil does it prefer?
faq.a: Acidic to neutral soils, including moist ones; avoid very chalky soils.

152.uses: Sessile oak is a valuable species for parks, afforestation, shelter belts and natural landscapes. Compared with English oak it copes better with dry, stony soils and slopes.
152.planting: It reaches 20–30 m with a broad, regular crown. Plant 10–12 m apart, or closer in afforestation. It prefers well-drained, acidic to neutral soils.
152.care: Water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: How does sessile oak differ from English oak?
faq.a: Its acorns sit almost directly on the twigs, and it copes better with dry, stony soils.

faq.q: Where is it used?
faq.a: In parks, afforestation, shelter belts and on slopes.

153.uses: The species is the classic tree for parks, estates, wide avenues and afforestation, with very high ecological value. 'Fastigiata Koster' has a narrow columnar crown and is used on streets, in car parks, at entrances and as a vertical accent.
153.planting: The species reaches 25–35 m with a broad crown; 'Fastigiata Koster' stays narrow (3–4 m). Plant the species 12–15 m apart, the columnar cultivar 4–6 m apart. It grows in almost any fertile soil, including clay and moist ones.
153.care: Water during the first years; oak roots deeply. Formative pruning in winter. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: What is 'Fastigiata Koster'?
faq.a: A columnar selection of oak with a narrow, dense crown, suitable for streets and narrow spaces.

faq.q: How long does an oak live?
faq.a: Oak can live for hundreds of years and is one of Europe's longest-lived trees.

154.uses: 'Frisia' is one of the brightest ornamental trees, with golden-yellow foliage all season. 'Bessoniana' has a compact, thornless oval crown suitable for streets, while 'Unifoliola' has larger leaves with few leaflets. 'Nyírségi' is a Hungarian selection with a straight trunk. All tolerate drought, heat and poor soils.
154.planting: They reach 10–15 m depending on the cultivar. In avenues plant 7–9 m apart. They grow in almost any well-drained soil, including sandy and dry ones.
154.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning in late summer. The wood is brittle, so correct crown training is important. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Which cultivar has yellow leaves?
faq.a: 'Frisia', with golden-yellow foliage from spring to autumn.

faq.q: Are there thornless cultivars?
faq.a: Yes, 'Bessoniana' and 'Unifoliola' are practically thornless and suit public spaces.

155.uses: 'Belders' is a Dutch selection of white willow with a regular crown, narrower than the species. It is planted along water, in moist parks, rural avenues and windbreaks.
155.planting: It reaches 15–20 m. Plant 6–10 m apart. It prefers moist soils, even temporarily flooded, in sun. Do not plant close to buildings and pipes.
155.care: It grows very fast and tolerates pruning well, including pollarding. Extremely frost hardy.

faq.q: Where is white willow planted?
faq.a: Along water, on moist soils and in temporarily flooded areas.

faq.q: How fast does it grow?
faq.a: Very fast – one of the quickest-growing species.

156.uses: One of the most decorative willows thanks to its glossy, aromatic foliage and late flowering. It is planted as a small tree in parks, by water, in moist gardens and naturalistic planting.
156.planting: It reaches 6–10 m with a rounded crown. Plant 5–6 m apart. It prefers moist, even boggy soils in sun or partial shade.
156.care: Water regularly on drier soils. Tolerates pruning well. Extremely frost hardy.

faq.q: Why is it called bay willow?
faq.a: Its leaves are glossy, dark green and slightly aromatic, like bay laurel.

faq.q: How big does it get?
faq.a: It is a small tree of 6–10 m.

157.uses: It is the best-known weeping willow, with golden branches that are decorative even in winter. It is planted as a specimen by lakes, ponds, rivers and in large parks, where its weeping silhouette reflects in the water.
157.planting: It reaches 12–15 m tall and as wide. It needs a lot of space. It prefers moist soils in sun. Do not plant near buildings, pipes or wells.
157.care: It grows fast. The branches can be shortened lightly to keep paths clear. Extremely frost hardy.

faq.q: Where should a weeping willow be planted?
faq.a: By water in large parks, where it has room for its broad weeping crown.

faq.q: Why are the branches yellow?
faq.a: 'Chrysocoma' has golden-yellow shoots, decorative even in winter without leaves.

158.uses: An excellent avenue tree for warm towns: it tolerates drought, heat reflected from paving and pollution. Its August flowering is an important nectar source for bees. 'Regent' has a regular oval crown and flowers earlier.
158.planting: It reaches 15–20 m with a broad, rounded crown. In avenues plant 8–10 m apart. It grows in almost any well-drained soil, including poor and dry ones.
158.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning in late summer. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Is it the same tree as Sophora japonica?
faq.a: Yes, Sophora japonica is the old name of Styphnolobium japonicum.

faq.q: When does it flower?
faq.a: In July–August, with large creamy-white panicles popular with bees.

159.uses: Standard Sorbus are ideal small trees for streets, car parks, gardens and parks: white spring blossom, fine foliage and berries that attract birds. 'Autumn Spire' has a narrow crown, 'Dodong' large leaves and red autumn colour, 'Edulis' large fruit usable once processed, while S. aria and S. intermedia have leaves silver beneath and tolerate drought.
159.planting: They reach 6–12 m depending on the cultivar. In avenues plant 5–7 m apart. They grow in most soils; S. aucuparia prefers slightly acidic soils, S. aria and S. intermedia tolerate chalky soils.
159.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Which Sorbus suits narrow streets?
faq.a: 'Autumn Spire', with a narrow columnar crown and orange autumn colour.

faq.q: Are the berries edible?
faq.a: The berries of 'Edulis' are larger and less bitter and are used for jams once processed.

160.uses: One of the best bee plants: its August flowers attract large numbers of bees and other pollinators. It is planted as a specimen or in groups in parks, gardens, pedestrian avenues and near apiaries.
160.planting: It reaches 8–12 m with a broad, rounded crown. Plant 6–8 m apart. It prefers well-drained soils in sun.
160.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Minimal pruning in winter. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Why is it called the bee-bee tree?
faq.a: It flowers in August with nectar-rich flowers, when bees find few other food sources.

faq.q: How big does it get?
faq.a: It is a small to medium-sized tree of 8–12 m.

161.uses: Hybrid limes are the traditional trees of European boulevards and parks. 'Pallida' has a regular conical crown suitable for avenues, 'Euchlora' has glossy leaves and is rarely attacked by aphids, so it does not drip sticky honeydew on cars and paving, and 'Glenleven' grows fast with a regular crown.
161.planting: They reach 15–25 m. In avenues plant 8–12 m apart. They prefer fertile, deep, well-drained soils.
161.care: They tolerate pruning very well, including roof-training and pleaching. Water during the first years. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Which lime does not drip sticky honeydew on cars?
faq.a: 'Euchlora' has glossy leaves and is rarely attacked by aphids, so it is recommended near car parks.

faq.q: When does lime flower?
faq.a: In June–July, with fragrant flowers that bees love.

162.uses: Modern elm cultivars such as 'Lutèce', 'Vada', 'Clusius' and 'Columella' were selected for resistance to Dutch elm disease and are robust avenue trees, tolerant of pollution, wind and salt. 'Columella' has a narrow columnar crown. European white elm (U. laevis) is valuable for moist areas, while 'Camperdownii' and 'Pendula' are weeping trees for gardens and parks.
162.planting: Avenue cultivars reach 15–25 m; 'Columella' stays narrow and the weeping forms small. In avenues plant 8–10 m apart. They grow in almost any soil.
162.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Very frost hardy.

faq.q: Are these elms disease resistant?
faq.a: 'Lutèce', 'Vada', 'Columella', 'Clusius' and 'Pioneer' were selected for high resistance to Dutch elm disease.

faq.q: Which cultivar suits narrow streets?
faq.a: 'Columella', with a very narrow columnar crown.

163.uses: Zelkova is an excellent avenue tree, related to elm but resistant to Dutch elm disease. Its vase-shaped crown leaves clear space beneath for pavements and car parks. 'Green Vase' grows fast with a regular crown, while 'Fastigiata' has a narrow crown for narrow streets.
163.planting: It reaches 15–20 m ('Fastigiata' stays narrow). In avenues plant 8–10 m apart ('Fastigiata' 4–6 m). It tolerates various soils, moderate drought and pollution.
163.care: Low maintenance; water during the first years. Formative pruning in winter. Hardy to about -25°C.

faq.q: Is zelkova resistant to Dutch elm disease?
faq.a: Yes, although related to elm, zelkova is highly resistant to Dutch elm disease.

faq.q: Which cultivar suits narrow streets?
faq.a: 'Fastigiata', with a narrow upright crown.
